Surpassing

sur-PASS-ing -- an adjective describing excellence, not the ordinary verb 'to surpass.' · adjective

Hear It

No recording available for this word.

What It Means

Surpassing is excelling or exceeding others.

Critics agreed the young violinist played with a surpassing grace that few professionals ever achieve.

Worked Example

A chef's signature dish is so far beyond anything else on the menu that food critics travel across the country just to taste it once.

That sense of standing far above every ordinary comparison is exactly what surpassing describes. Unlike 'decent,' which is simply acceptable, surpassing means truly extraordinary.

Antonyms

mediocre

inferior

inferior: lower in quality or ability

How Strong Is It? — exceptional → peerless → surpassing

exceptional vs. surpassing

exceptional vs. surpassing: Exceptional is a bit milder than surpassing -- exceptional simply means unusually good, while surpassing specifically emphasizes standing above every direct comparison.

peerless vs. surpassing

peerless vs. surpassing: Peerless can feel even stronger than surpassing: surpassing means excelling beyond others, while peerless suggests there is truly no equal to be found anywhere.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — sur-

prefix — sur-: over, above (Old French (from Latin super))

root — -pass-

root — -pass-: to pass, go beyond (Old French (passer))

suffix — -ing

suffix — -ing: forming an adjective from a verb (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Old French sur- ('above, beyond') plus passer ('to pass'), with the -ing ending turning the verb into an adjective. Something surpassing has passed beyond every ordinary measure -- the same root gives us bypass.

Use the root in a new word: bypass

Use the root in a new word: bypass: Engineers built a new bypass so trucks could avoid driving straight through the crowded town center.

Root Check

Word Choice

Surpassing is a formal, literary adjective usually paired with an admirable quality, as in 'surpassing talent,' 'surpassing beauty,' or 'surpassing skill' -- it does not describe an action the way the verb 'surpass' does.
